paper_title: Knowledge Crosswords Geometric Knowledge Reasoning with Large Language   Models
caption: Problem distribution based on the correctness under the w/ knowledge and w/o knowledge settings using CoT and . The results indicate that while easier problems are mainly hindered by a lack of knowledge, the bottleneck for hard problems lies in geometric knowledge reasoning abilities.
model_annotation: The figure presents three pie charts—labeled “easy,” “medium,” and “hard”—each illustrating the distribution of problem outcomes based on whether the model had access to knowledge (N+K+ or N–K+) or not (N+K– or N–K–), under the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning setting. A shared legend indicates four categories: teal for N+K+ (with knowledge, correct), beige for N–K+ (without knowledge, correct), orange for N–K– (without knowledge, incorrect), and red for N+K– (with knowledge, incorrect). In the “easy” chart, the largest segment is beige (45.9%, N–K+), followed by teal (40.6%, N+K+), then orange (10.1%, N–K–), and a small red slice (3.3%, N+K–). The “medium” chart shows near-equal shares of teal (44.6%, N+K+) and beige (44.3%, N–K+), with smaller orange (7.2%, N–K–) and red (3.9%, N+K–) slices. In the “hard” chart, orange (36.8%, N–K–) and beige (36.2%, N–K+) dominate, followed by teal (20.1%, N+K+) and red (7.0%, N+K–). The visual trend suggests that for easy problems, correctness is often achieved even without knowledge, while for hard problems, the majority of failures occur regardless of knowledge availability, pointing to reasoning as the limiting factor.
